chapter.title: What is left: the owners' share

cards.body: Can a business owe more than everything it owns and still open its doors at 7am tomorrow? Yes, and the house shows how. Take what the house is worth, subtract the mortgage, and what's left is **your share**. On a balance sheet that share is called *equity*.
cards.simpler: Can a business owe more than everything it owns and still open its doors at 7am tomorrow? Yes. A house helps show how. Take what your house is worth and subtract what you still owe on the mortgage, the loan you used to buy it. What's left over is **your share**. A balance sheet, the page listing what a business owns and owes, calls that share *equity*.

cards.prompt: Ana bought a £200,000 flat with a £30,000 deposit. Five years on, the flat is still valued at £200,000 and the mortgage is down to £160,000. How much of the flat is Ana's?

whyNot.a: That's what the flat is worth, not what's left after the mortgage: take off the £160,000 still owed.
whyNot.c: That's what Ana put in at the start, not the share today: paying down the mortgage added £10,000 more.

cards.reteach: Your share is always what you own minus what you owe. £200,000 minus £160,000 leaves £40,000. The deposit was only where it started.

cards.title: Two pipes fill it
cards.body:
Equity is filled by **two pipes**. The first is money the owners put in, like the deposit on the house. On a real sheet it's often called *share capital*: the cash people paid the company for their shares.

The second pipe is profit the company kept instead of handing out. That's *retained earnings* (retained just means held on to). Think of spare pay going into a new kitchen instead of a holiday.

When owners take money out as *dividends* (cash paid to shareholders), the second pipe drains a little.
cards.simpler: Equity gets filled by **two pipes**. The first is money the owners put in, like the deposit you pay on a house. Company records often call this *share capital*, the cash people paid for their shares. The second pipe is profit the company kept instead of handing out, called *retained earnings*. It's like spending spare pay on a new kitchen rather than a holiday. When owners take cash out as *dividends*, this second pipe drains a little.

cards.title: A coffee cart, two years
cards.body: Dev puts £20,000 into a coffee cart company. Year one makes £8,000 profit, Dev takes £5,000 out as a dividend, £3,000 stays in, and equity is now £23,000. Year two brings a wet summer and a broken espresso machine: a £10,000 loss. Equity drops to £13,000, even though Dev never took back a penny of the original £20,000. Losses come out of the same pot as kept profit.
cards.simpler: Dev puts £20,000 into a coffee cart company. In year one it makes £8,000 profit. Dev takes £5,000 out as a dividend and leaves £3,000 in, so equity grows to £23,000. Year two brings a wet summer and a broken espresso machine, and the cart loses £10,000. Equity falls to £13,000, even though Dev never took back a penny of the first £20,000. **Losses come out of the same pot** as kept profit.

cards.prompt: Hollow Oak Ltd's owners put in £50m. Over ten years it made £80m in profit and paid £60m of that out as dividends. Roughly what does its equity line show?

whyNot.a: That's money in plus all the profit, not the profit kept: the £60m paid out has left the pot.
whyNot.c: That's only the first pipe, not both: the £20m of kept profit belongs to the owners too.

cards.reteach: Equity is money put in plus profit kept. Profit kept is £80m made minus £60m paid out, so £20m. Add the owners' £50m and you get £70m.

cards.title: Below zero, and not a price tag
cards.body:
Drain the second pipe hard enough and equity drops **below zero**. Years of losses can do it. So can paying owners more than the business has kept, often through *buybacks*, where a company buys its own shares back. McDonald's has shown negative equity in recent years, largely for that reason, and still serves breakfast every morning.

You'd think equity tells you what a company is worth. It doesn't. It's a record of history: what owners put in and kept, counted at what things cost. A buyer pays for what the business will earn next. That can be far more, or far less.
cards.simpler: Drain the second pipe hard enough and equity falls **below zero**. Years of losses can do it. So can paying owners more than the business kept, often by buying back its own shares. McDonald's has shown negative equity lately, largely for this reason, yet still serves breakfast. Equity isn't a price tag. It records what owners put in and kept, at what things cost. A buyer pays for what the business will earn, which can be far more or less.

cards.body: Mia sees a company showing £4bn of equity, notices its shares add up to only £3bn on the stock market, and calls it a bargain. But that £4bn is built from what its factories cost years ago, not what anyone would pay for them today. Spot it: if you're treating equity as a price tag, stop. **It's what went in and stayed, not what it would sell for.**
cards.simpler: Mia sees a company with £4bn of equity. On the stock market, all its shares together are worth only £3bn, so she calls it a bargain. But that £4bn is built from what its factories cost years ago, not what anyone would pay for them today. Here's the warning sign: if you're treating equity as a price tag, stop. **It's what went in and stayed, not what it would sell for.**

cards.prompt: A well-known chain reports equity of minus £2bn, yet its shops are busy and it pays its bills. What's the likeliest story?

options.text: It's quietly bankrupt and will close within the year.
Over the years it paid out more to owners than they put in plus the profit it kept.
Its share price has fallen below zero.

whyNot.a: That's reading equity as a verdict, not a history: negative equity alone doesn't mean it can't pay.
whyNot.c: That's the market price, not the equity line: equity comes from the company's own records, and share prices can't go below zero.

cards.reteach: Equity is money in plus profit kept, minus what's been paid out. Pay out more than that and the line dips under zero. It tells you where money went, not that the doors are closing.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
The owners' share is the money they put in plus the profit the company kept, and losses and payouts shrink it, sometimes **below zero**. It's a record of the past, not the price anyone would pay for the business.

Tomorrow: three checks in five minutes that spot trouble before a profitable company runs dry.
cards.simpler: The owners' share is the money they put in plus the profit the company kept. Losses and payouts to owners shrink it, sometimes **below zero**. Think of it as a record of the past, not the price anyone would pay for the business. Tomorrow you'll learn three checks that take five minutes and spot trouble before a profitable company runs out of cash.

cards.body: Search any big company's name plus 'balance sheet'. In the equity section, find the money owners put in (often 'share capital') and 'retained earnings'. Which pipe is bigger?
cards.simpler: Try this. Search for any big company's name plus 'balance sheet'. Find the equity section, the part showing the owners' share. Look for the money owners put in, often labelled 'share capital', and for 'retained earnings', the profit the company kept. Then compare them. **Which pipe is bigger?**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain where a company's equity number came from and say whether past profits were kept or paid out.
